From its corner the lamb’s severed head Watches the flies drink from its eyes And its fat disappear into the fire. The light rinses the edge of your sandal, The two wasps that ornament the blur Of screened window. My grandmother Would have loved a night like this. In the wind chimes I can hear her tea cart With its china rolling through Cook Street’s Stony yard one summer when I was always Thirsty, and she moved like a figure On a clock from my lawn chair to the cart, Or swabbed me with alcohol, or cut My hair with the straight razor. I was a week out of the hospital. Beneath my breasts an incision was crossed With stitches of surgical thread. The scalpel came so close it gave My heart a quick kiss. I nearly died. outputs.L1:
In Tunis, we attempt to speak of divorce and mortality, but eventually yield to the afternoon, lounging alongside rug merchants beneath the shade of a plum tree. From its corner, a lamb’s severed head observes flies drinking from its eyes while its fat drips and disappears into the fire. Sunlight rinses the edge of your sandal, catching the two wasps that adorn the blurred mesh of the screened window. 

My grandmother would have cherished a night such as this. In the sound of the wind chimes, I can hear her china tea cart rolling across the stony yard of Cook Street during a summer when I was perpetually thirsty. She moved with the steady precision of a clockwork figure, pacing between my lawn chair and her cart—swabbing my skin with rubbing alcohol or trimming my hair with a straight razor. 

I was only a week out of the hospital at the time. Beneath my breasts, a fresh incision was crisscrossed with surgical thread; the scalpel had come so dangerously close that it imparted a brief kiss to my heart. I nearly died. 

Years later, I can still see the skin flutter over the inner slope of my left breast, where my heart now limps like a great-uncle who—because he was lame and a Jew—was dragged by Cossacks across the steppes. In his ordeal, he became like a friend asking a favor of a horse that ran so furiously, so exquisitely hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.

Here is a well-structured narrative expansion based on your bullet points:

***

In Tunis, the sun has a way of softening life’s harsher edges. For days, my companion and I had been trapped in exhausting, circular conversations about the quiet catastrophe of divorce and the looming specter of our own mortality. Eventually, worn down by the weight of our grief, we surrendered to the afternoon. We abandoned our heavy talk and retreated outdoors, finding a shaded table near a bustling market. There, amidst the ambient rhythm of local merchants calling out their wares, the scent of roasting spices, and the warmth of the Mediterranean breeze, we finally allowed ourselves to simply rest.

Sitting in that golden light, the sensory calm triggered a sudden, vivid memory. I was abruptly transported back to a distant childhood, lying confined to a bedroom filled with the soft, attentive presence of my grandmother. During a prolonged period of severe illness, she had been my quiet guardian. I remembered the cool touch of her hand on my forehead and the ceaseless, devoted care with which she shepherded me through the darkest days of my youth.

It was during that fragile summer that I had undergone a near-fatal surgical procedure. The doctors managed to pull me back from the brink of death, but the operation left a permanent monument on my body: a long, pale incision etched into my chest, running dangerously close to my heart. The body healed, but it carried the physical evidence of how narrowly I had escaped.

Decades later, the physical legacy of that day still lingers beneath my ribs. My heart has never quite recovered its proper cadence; it beats with a peculiar, off-kilter hitch—a sudden falter before catching its rhythm again. Whenever I feel that erratic thrum, I am reminded of my family’s stories about my Jewish great-uncle. As a young man in the old country, he had been captured by Cossacks and violently dragged across the frozen steppes behind a galloping horse. He survived the ordeal, but for the rest of his life, he walked with a pronounced, halting limp. 

My damaged heart moves through time in the exact same way—a resilient, battered survivor, forever limping through its beats, carrying both its own scar and the echoed trauma of the past.
outputs.L4:
The Mediterranean sun washes over Tunis in shades of bleached white and terra cotta. In a quiet courtyard, the afternoon air smells of crushed jasmine, dark coffee, and the faint, salty breeze blowing off the gulf. Time here moves with a slow, deliberate rhythm; the shadow of a palm frond traces a lazy arc across the painted tiles, offering a peace so absolute it almost feels unearned. Yet, even in the midst of this tranquil sanctuary, my body remains a repository for an older, darker geography. 

Beneath the warmth of the North African sun, a sudden, phantom chill can settle in the center of my chest. Unconsciously, my fingers reach up to trace the long, pale ridge running down my sternum—a silver seam sewn shut when I was only seven years old. 

In a heartbeat, the serenity of Tunis dissolves, replaced by the sensory ghosts of a childhood open-heart surgery. I am pulled back to the blinding, sterile white of the operating theater, the sharp metallic tang of anesthesia, and the terrifying silence that preceded the scalpels. I remember—or perhaps my nerves remember for me—the sensation of a small, flawed heart being temporarily stilled, resting in the cold, gloved hands of strangers while a machine hummed to keep the rest of me alive. To survive such an ordeal as a child is to acquire a premature literacy in mortality. It teaches you that the thread tying you to this world is astonishingly thin, capable of being severed, mended, and knotted by human hands.

Yet, as I sit listening to the distant call to prayer floating over the rooftops of the Medina, I realize that this physical vulnerability does not belong to me alone. The scar on my chest is not merely a private artifact of modern medicine; it is a continuation of a far older lineage. 

I carry the memory of my ancestors in the very rhythm of this repaired heart. I think of the generations before me who weathered their own silent catastrophes—those who survived displacement, epidemic, war, and the quiet, crushing weight of grief. They, too, lived in close proximity to death, feeling its cold breath against their necks while stubbornly continuing the work of living. The bodily trauma I endured in that operating room was not an anomaly in my bloodline, but an echo. My body recognized the fight because it had been rehearsed for generations.

Medical science speaks of healing as a total restoration, a return to a baseline of health. But the body does not forget being opened to the sky. The physical and emotional scars of near-death survival do not simply fade into background noise; they linger stubbornly in the nerve endings, in a sudden spike of panic at a sterile smell, in the quiet hesitation before taking a deep breath. Survival is not a clean escape from death, but a permanent negotiation with it. The body remains marked, a physical testament to the moment it was forced to choose between yielding or enduring.

Here in Tunis, surrounded by ancient stones that have themselves survived centuries of conquest, collapse, and rebirth, the juxtaposition becomes clear. The quiet moments of the present are not a negation of past trauma, but a frame for it. My heart beats today with a complex, borrowed strength—forged by surgical steel, sustained by modern skill, and fueled by an ancestral grit that refused to be extinguished. We do not carry our scars despite our survival; we carry them as proof of an unbroken, intergenerational legacy of resilience, forever reminding us of the price—and the quiet triumph—of remaining alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem that moves from a modern scene in Tunis to childhood memories of recovering from a near-fatal surgery, ending with a family legend about a Jewish ancestor on the steppes.
counterfactuals.output:
The sun over the Gulf of Tunis is a heavy, golden coin
slid across sea-salt and whitewashed stone.
Here on the balcony, chicory coffee cools beside a bowl of figs,
and the scent of crushed jasmine drifts up from the courtyard,
thick as sleep.
Down on the avenue, a red tram clangs past the scalloped arches,
and a boy sells mint leaves from a woven basket,
his voice rising into the heat.

I touch my ribcage through the thin linen of my shirt,
feeling the pale, puckered thread beneath my skin—
the scar that still pulls when the weather turns humid.

Thirty years ago, in a season made entirely of bleach and ether,
that line was a fresh, violet river.
I remember the seven-year-old darkness,
the heavy, mechanical click of monitors in the night,
and the cold, terrifying stillness of a room 
where my breathing was kept on a leash.
I remember hovering near the ceiling, watching my own small hands,
translucent as wax against the hospital sheets,
while the surgeons spoke in muted tones of improbable odds.
My mother sat by the window, her lips moving without sound,
stitching me back to the earth with her silence.
When I finally woke, coughing up the taste of copper,
the pain was a blinding light,
a reminder that the body is a cage of bone
we must fight to stay inside.

My mother would smooth my damp hair back then and tell me 
that my blood was too stubborn to spill,
that it carried the cold iron of the old world.

She spoke of him—the legend we kept like a silver coin in a pocket—
the Great-Uncle Avram, or perhaps his father before him,
a Jewish peddler on the boundless, wind-scoured steppes.
Long before our name found the warm waters of this coast,
he rode between the mud-bound villages of Ukraine,
a tailor carrying a box of brass buttons and a velvet bag of tefillin.
The story goes that when the winter broke like glass
and the Cossacks swept through the tall feathergrass,
he hid beneath the floorboards of an abandoned mill,
eating snow and dry crusts for seven days,
his feet wrapped in burlap, his frostbitten fingers 
still holding the needle he used to sew his prayers into his coat.
They say he bargained with a wolf-eyed soldier using a single psalm,
or perhaps just the sheer, terrifying audacity of his living eyes,
and walked out onto the white desert of grass, unbroken.

I sit now in the shade of a Tunisian palm,
the Mediterranean hummed to a bright, turquoise glow.
The wind coming off the water is soft, carrying no frost, no formaldehyde—
only the warmth of a world that kept turning.
I take a breath, deep and easy,
filling the lungs that once refused to work,
feeling the steppe-wind in my chest,
endless, wild, and saved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a contemporary narrative poem exploring themes of mortality, body scars, and generational memory. Include vivid sensory details like a severed lamb's head, wind chimes sounding like a tea cart, and a heart surgery incision.
counterfactuals.output:
On the back porch, the afternoon sours to silver.  
The aluminum chimes suspended from the eaves  
shiver in a sudden mountain draft—clinking light and urgent,  
sounding like a tea cart wheeled over uneven flagstones,  
porcelain cups and silver spoons rattling against the tray.  
My father sits in the low wicker chair,  
his breath a wet, slow bellows catching on the turn of the air.  

His linen shirt sags open at the throat.  
There, dividing his chest, runs the scar:  
a raised, keloid ridge, pale as bleached hemp,  
stretching from his collarbone down to the pit of his stomach.  
It is the zipper left behind by the saw  
that once parted his sternum like a pine crate,  
allowing stranger's hands to reach inside  
and mend the frayed muscle of his heart.  
In the slant sunlight, the seam catches the glare—  
a vertical line of longitude mapping where he almost ended,  
the quiet rift where his mortality broke through the skin.  

He touches his sternum absentmindedly,  
his thumb trailing the smooth, hairless cleft,  
and I know his mind is sinking backward, slipping  
through the trapdoor of blood and inheritance.  
He is thinking of his own father, sixty years dead,  
and a freezing dawn in the autumn of nineteen-fifty-eight.  

He tells me again of the block behind the smokehouse,  
the smell of wet wool, manure, and turnip greens.  
He remembers the dull, heavy *thud* of the iron cleaver  
and the severed lamb’s head lying in the frozen clover—  
its cloudy, pale-blue eye still open, staring fixedly  
at the woodpile, tongue pinned between grey teeth,  
and the faint, blue steam rising from the wet stump of its neck  
into the sharp November frost.  
*That was the day,* he whispers, his voice like dry leaves,  
*I realized how little holds a breath inside a chest.*  

The wind chimes shudder again, rolling their porcelain chime  
across the roofline, a ghost pushing tea into a quiet room.  
My father lays his hand over his scarred chest,  
as if holding the halves of himself together.  

I reach out and place my hand over his knuckles,  
feeling the thick, ropey pulse beneath his paper skin.  
I have no scar like his—not yet—  
but I feel the weight of the lamb’s head in my own throat,  
the cold steel of the cleaver in my bones,  
and the saw that waits for every family tree.  
Generations do not pass down land or gold so much as wounds:  
the way the body learns to close around its cuts,  
stitching memory into flesh, pretending the seam was always there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about living with a surgical scar near your heart and how it makes you feel connected to your family's history of survival.
counterfactuals.output:
It sits two inches from the pulse,
a silver seam, a raised embossed line—
where steel and suture met my flesh
to alter what was once design.
A quiet ridge across my chest,
a mark where shadow met the light,
the sudden thread that holds the heart
and keeps it pushing through the night.

When fingers trace this altered skin,
I do not feel a sense of loss;
I feel the weight of those who came
and bore their own unwritten cross.
My bloodline was not built of glass;
'twas forged in iron, shaped by storm.
My elders walked through winter’s wrath
to keep the coming embers warm.

My grandfather bore hidden marks,
a piece of war beneath his knee.
My grandmother wore quiet lines
of grief she would not let us see.
They survived the famine, crossed the sea,
they bent beneath the heavy yield,
yet every wound became a seed
that planted me inside this field.

So when my own heart faltered once,
and surgeons cut to pull me through,
they only did what heritage asked—
they mended what the lineage knew.
They stitched the vessel, bound the tear,
and handed back my borrowed breath,
a testament that in our house,
we choose the morning over death.

I touch the scar. I feel the drum
that echoes back a century.
I am the sum of all who fought
to leave a living heart in me.
This line is not a mark of flaw,
nor proof of how I almost fell—
it is the crest of my redeemers,
the stubborn song of staying well.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, evocative poem using the following prompt elements: rug merchants under a plum tree in Tunis, flies on a slaughtered lamb, a grandmother cutting hair with a straight razor, and a lame great uncle fleeing Cossacks.
counterfactuals.output:
Under the bruised, overripe shade of a plum tree in Tunis,
the rug merchants unspool their dark geometry.
They trade in heavy wool, dyed in indigo and madder,
fingering the thick pile where shadows gather like oil.
The fruit above them drops, soft and split,
bleeding sweet rot into the dust.

A stone’s throw away, a slaughtered lamb hangs inverted,
its ribcage opened like a vaulted ceiling.
A black swarm of flies hums a wet, rhythmic vesper,
drinking from the tallow, trailing iridescent green
across the quiet, cooling muscle of the meat.
Blood drips—a slow, crimson counting of seconds.

Time is a carpet folded back on itself.
In the cool pantry of another life, Grandmother stands,
unclasping the silver handle of her straight razor.
She scrapes the nape of a neck with terrible precision,
the steel whispering against skin, cold and absolute.
Shorn locks fall like dark feathers to the floorboards,
each stroke a quiet cut between survival and slaughter.

Her hand does not tremble; it was steeled long ago,
watching her uncle—lame from birth, his hip a twisted knot—
stumble through the freezing wheat of the steppes.
Behind him, the earth shook with Cossack hooves,
the air shrill with whistling sabers and the scent of burning oats.
He ran on one good leg and a dragging limp,
a ragged shape fleeing the flash of iron,
dragging his shadow all the way to the southern sea.

Now, in the heat of the souk, the threads entangle:
the flies on the lamb, the razor at the throat,
the uneven drag of a dead man’s boot in the snow.
The merchants knot the silk with stained, patient thumbs,
weaving the terror into patterns,
and sell it to strangers to lay beneath their feet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a deeply sensory reflective poem about childhood convalescence and bodily fragility.
counterfactuals.output:
The room smelled of camphor and dried chamomile,
of heavy wool blankets saturated with sleep.
Outside, the afternoon unspooled its pale, thin light;
inside, the stillness ran ten fathoms deep.
I lay as a small thing moored in damp linen,
watching dust motes drift like suspended snow,
my fever a low hearth burning in the dark—
a quiet, stubborn fire I did not choose to know.

My skin turned translucent, a lantern of porcelain,
where blue veins branched like winter-bare trees.
I learned the light architecture of my own small bones,
the fragile, aching hinges of elbows and knees.
A silver spoon would clink against my teeth—
salty broth gleaming with amber drops of fat,
my mouth tasting of iron and boiled pear,
my pulse a bruised bird where my wrist lay flat.

Through the shut window came the ghost of the world:
the dull thud of a ball, a neighbor’s distant shout.
How strange to think of legs that ran and leaped,
while all my vigor was slowly draining out.
The sunlight dragged across the rose-patterned wall,
ticking in inches like a shadow-clock,
shifting from marigold to slate-gray gloom,
until the floorboards creaked beneath a mother's walk.

Her hand was a leaf of cool winter air
pressed to the dry terrain of my flushed brow.
She brought the damp towel smelling of lavender and rain,
and whispered *hush*, though I was silent now.
Bound in that soft realm between the ache and mend,
I felt the secret, mortal truth take hold:
that we are built of dust and fragile thread,
and warmth is just a thing we borrow from the cold.
